Sandals
SAN-dlz
n. pl. (soles bound to the foot with thongs; the footwear of the Twelve and of Peter's deliverance)
Greek sandalion, a small board, through Latin. The Authorized Version uses the word twice, both in the New Testament: in the Lord's instructions to the Twelve and in the angel's instructions to Peter in the prison.

Biblical Definition

But be shod with sandals; and not put on two coats. The Lord is sending out the Twelve two by two, and the outfitting is deliberately meagre: nothing for the journey save a staff only, no scrip, no bread, no money in their purse, and one coat apiece. Sandals are permitted because a man must walk; a second coat is not, because a second coat is a margin against depending on God and on the households that receive them. The other occurrence is in a prison at night. The angel said unto him, Gird thyself, and bind on thy sandals. And so he did. And he saith unto him, Cast thy garment about thee, and follow me. Peter is chained between two soldiers, the church is praying in Mary's house, and the rescue proceeds through an ordinary sequence of getting dressed. Even in a miracle a man ties his own shoes. The two passages together hold the dictionary's doctrine of ordinary means and extraordinary grace in one homely object, and Paul supplies the figure that gathers them: your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a kind of shoe, consisting of a sole fastened to the foot; in Scripture, the footwear permitted to the Twelve and bound on by Peter at his deliverance.

expand to see more

SANDAL, n. A kind of shoe, consisting of a sole fastened to the foot with strings or thongs.

SHOD, pp. Furnished with shoes; having shoes on the feet.

SCRIP, n. A small bag; a wallet; a satchel carried by travellers and shepherds.

GIRD, v.t. To bind by surrounding with any flexible substance, as a belt or cord.

PROVISION, n. The act of providing or making previous preparation; measures taken beforehand.

Key Scripture

Mar 6:9 — "But be shod with sandals; and not put on two coats."

Mar 6:8 — "And commanded them that they should take nothing for their journey, save a staff only; no scrip, no bread, no money in their purse."

Act 12:8 — "And the angel said unto him, Gird thyself, and bind on thy sandals. And so he did. And he saith unto him, Cast thy garment about thee, and follow me."

Eph 6:15 — "And your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace;"

Modern Corruption

The mission instructions of Mark 6 are taken either as a rule of permanent poverty binding on every minister or as a quaint detail with no application; the Lord gave them for a particular sending and himself revised the terms later.

expand to see more

The Twelve were sent out with a staff and sandals and no bread, and they lacked nothing. But in Luke 22 the Lord asks them, when I sent you without purse, and scrip, and shoes, lacked ye any thing? And they said, Nothing. And then he says, But now, he that hath a purse, let him take it, and likewise his scrip. The same Lord who stripped them down re-equipped them for a different season. A rule read out of Mark 6 as a permanent law of ministerial destitution ignores that revision, and a reading that finds nothing binding in it ignores the principle underneath, which is that the labourer is worthy of his hire and that God provides for the men he sends through the people he sends them to.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, and the principle to recover is dependence without presumption. Peter's night in prison shows the same balance from the other side: God sends an angel, opens the iron gate of his own accord, and still tells the man to put his shoes on and walk. The church meanwhile is praying and does not believe the answer when it knocks at the door. Ordinary obedience and extraordinary deliverance are not rivals in Scripture; they are almost always found in the same room.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek sandalion (G4547), a sandal; hupodeo (G5265), to bind under the foot, to shoe; chiton (G5509), an inner garment or coat.

expand to see more

Greek sandalion (G4547) — a sandal, a sole bound to the foot; both occurrences are New Testament.

Greek hupodeo (G5265) — to bind beneath, to put on shoes; be shod with sandals.

Greek chiton (G5509) — a tunic or inner coat; and not put on two coats.

Greek pera (G4082) — a wallet or provision bag; no scrip.

Greek hetoimasia (G2091) — readiness, preparation; the preparation of the gospel of peace.

Usage

"“But be shod with sandals” — the Twelve sent out with almost nothing."

"“Gird thyself, and bind on thy sandals” — the angel's words in the prison."

"“your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace” — the armour figure."
